notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Social geography studies the spatial distribution of people and social groups.
  • It examines relationships between society and geographical space.
  • Important themes include:
  • Language.
  • Tribal communities.
  • Settlements.
  • Migration.
  • Rural and urban society.
  • Cultural regions.
  • Human adaptation to environment.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Social Geography → People + Society + Space

2. Human Diversity of India

India has great social and cultural diversity because of:

  • Large geographical extent.
  • Long history of migration.
  • Mountain barriers.
  • River valleys.
  • Coastal connections.
  • Different climates.
  • Regional historical development.
3. Unity in Diversity — Geographical Basis

India contains major differences in:

  • Languages.
  • Food habits.
  • Clothing.
  • Settlement patterns.
  • Occupations.
  • Customs.

Despite this diversity, transport, trade, political integration and cultural interaction connect different regions.

4. Social Geography and Physical Geography

Physical geography influences society through:

  • Climate.
  • Relief.
  • Water availability.
  • Natural vegetation.
  • Soil.
  • Resources.
5. Geography and Occupation

Examples include:

  • Coastal communities → Fishing.
  • Mountain communities → Pastoralism and horticulture.
  • Fertile plains → Agriculture.
  • Mineral regions → Mining and industry.
  • Cities → Manufacturing and services.
6. Cultural Landscape
  • A cultural landscape is a landscape modified by human activity.
  • Examples include:
  • Agricultural fields.
  • Settlements.
  • Temples.
  • Roads.
  • Irrigation tanks.
  • Plantation landscapes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Cultural Landscape → Nature Modified by Humans

7. Settlement Geography

Human settlements are broadly classified into:

  • Rural settlements.
  • Urban settlements.
8. Rural Settlement
  • Rural settlements are generally associated with:
  • Agriculture.
  • Animal husbandry.
  • Forestry.
  • Fishing.
  • Other primary activities.
9. Urban Settlement
  • Urban settlements generally have a larger concentration of:
  • Non-agricultural occupations.
  • Industries.
  • Trade.
  • Services.
  • Administrative functions.
10. Rural Settlement Patterns

Important settlement patterns include:

  • Compact or nucleated.
  • Dispersed.
  • Linear.
  • Circular.
  • Rectangular.
11. Compact Settlement
  • Houses are grouped closely together.
  • Compact settlements are common in fertile plains and areas where people share common resources.
12. Dispersed Settlement
  • Houses are scattered over a wide area.
  • They are common in:
  • Hilly terrain.
  • Forest regions.
  • Large farm areas.
13. Linear Settlement
  • Houses develop along:
  • Roads.
  • Rivers.
  • Canals.
  • Coastlines.
  • Railway lines.
📌 Must-Memorise

Linear Settlement → Along a Route or Physical Feature

14. Circular Settlement
  • Houses may develop around:
  • A tank.
  • Lake.
  • Fort.
  • Temple.
  • Common open space.
15. Settlement and Water
  • Availability of water is one of the strongest controls of settlement.
  • Villages frequently develop near:
  • Rivers.
  • Tanks.
  • Wells.
  • Springs.
16. Settlement and Relief

Plains:

  • Larger and more compact settlements.

Mountains:

  • Smaller and more dispersed settlements.
17. Settlement and Security

Historically, settlements were sometimes concentrated around:

  • Forts.
  • Elevated sites.
  • Walled towns.

for protection.

18. Site and Situation

Site:

  • Actual physical location of a settlement.

Situation:

  • Location of the settlement relative to surrounding places and routes.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Site ≠ Situation

19. Rural–Urban Continuum
  • Rural and urban areas are not completely separate.
  • Peri-urban regions often contain characteristics of both.
20. Rural–Urban Linkages

Rural and urban areas exchange:

  • Food.
  • Labour.
  • Manufactured goods.
  • Services.
  • Capital.
  • Information.
21. Social Groups and Geography

Different social groups may show distinctive geographic patterns because of:

  • Historical migration.
  • Occupations.
  • Ecology.
  • Cultural traditions.
  • Political boundaries.
22. Race — Modern Scientific Caution
  • Older geography textbooks often classified Indian populations into "racial groups" based on physical characteristics.
  • Modern genetics shows that human populations are highly mixed and cannot be divided into rigid biological races.
  • TNPSC questions may still use older anthropological classifications, so they should be treated as historical classification systems rather than fixed biological divisions.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Traditional Racial Classification → Historical Anthropological Model, Not Rigid Modern Genetic Categories

23. Traditional Anthropological Classification of Indian Population

Older classifications commonly referred to groups such as:

  • Negrito.
  • Proto-Australoid.
  • Mongoloid.
  • Mediterranean.
  • Western Brachycephals.
  • Nordic.

These classifications overlap and should not be interpreted as pure or isolated populations.

24. Negrito — Traditional Classification

Older anthropology associated Negrito characteristics with small populations in:

  • Andaman Islands.
  • Some isolated forest populations were historically compared with this category.
25. Andamanese Communities

Important indigenous communities of the Andaman Islands include:

  • Great Andamanese.
  • Onge.
  • Jarawa.
  • Sentinelese.
📌 Must-Memorise

Andaman Tribes → Great Andamanese + Onge + Jarawa + Sentinelese

26. Sentinelese
  • Sentinelese live on North Sentinel Island.
  • They are one of the world's most isolated indigenous communities.
  • Their isolation has limited outside contact.
27. Jarawa
  • Jarawa traditionally inhabit parts of the Andaman Islands.
  • They have historically depended on hunting and gathering.
28. Onge
  • Onge are associated mainly with Little Andaman Island.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Onge → Little Andaman

29. Great Andamanese
  • Great Andamanese historically inhabited several Andaman islands.
  • Their population declined greatly following outside contact.
30. Proto-Australoid — Traditional Classification

Older anthropological literature associated Proto-Australoid characteristics with many tribal populations of central and eastern India.

Regions frequently mentioned include:

  • Chotanagpur Plateau.
  • Central India.
  • Eastern Ghats.
31. Mongoloid — Traditional Classification

Older anthropological classifications associated Mongoloid characteristics primarily with populations of:

  • Northeastern India.
  • Himalayan regions.
32. Himalayan and Northeast Populations

Geographical isolation and historical connections with Tibet and Southeast Asia contributed to distinctive cultural and linguistic patterns in northeastern and Himalayan regions.

33. Mediterranean — Traditional Classification

Older classifications associated Mediterranean-related populations with large portions of the Indian subcontinent.

34. Nordic — Traditional Classification

Older anthropological models associated Nordic characteristics with some northwestern populations.

35. Why Traditional Racial Categories Are Limited
  • Indian populations have experienced migration and intermixture for thousands of years.
  • Physical features vary continuously rather than forming strict boundaries.
  • Linguistic, tribal and cultural identities are more useful for many geography questions.
36. Language Geography of India
  • India is one of the world's most linguistically diverse countries.
  • Language distribution reflects:
  • Migration.
  • History.
  • Regional isolation.
  • Political development.
37. Major Language Families of India

Four major language-family groups commonly discussed are:

  • Indo-Aryan.
  • Dravidian.
  • Austroasiatic.
  • Tibeto-Burman.
📌 Must-Memorise

Indian Language Families → Indo-Aryan + Dravidian + Austroasiatic + Tibeto-Burman

38. Indo-Aryan Languages
  • Indo-Aryan languages belong to the Indo-European language family.
  • They dominate much of northern, western and eastern India.
39. Major Indo-Aryan Languages

Important examples include:

  • Hindi.
  • Bengali.
  • Marathi.
  • Gujarati.
  • Punjabi.
  • Assamese.
  • Odia.
  • Urdu.
  • Konkani.
  • Kashmiri.
  • Sindhi.
40. Hindi
  • Hindi is widely spoken across northern and central India.
  • It belongs to the Indo-Aryan branch.
41. Bengali
  • Bengali is spoken mainly in:
  • West Bengal.
  • Parts of eastern and northeastern India.
  • It is also the major language of Bangladesh.
42. Marathi
  • Marathi is the principal language of Maharashtra.
  • It belongs to the Indo-Aryan family.
43. Gujarati
  • Gujarati is the principal regional language of Gujarat.
  • It belongs to the Indo-Aryan family.
44. Punjabi
  • Punjabi is widely spoken in Punjab.
  • It belongs to the Indo-Aryan family.
45. Odia
  • Odia is the major regional language of Odisha.
  • It belongs to the Indo-Aryan family.
46. Assamese
  • Assamese is widely spoken in the Brahmaputra Valley of Assam.
  • It belongs to the Indo-Aryan family.
47. Dravidian Languages
  • Dravidian languages are concentrated mainly in southern India.
  • They also occur among some populations outside southern India.
48. Four Major Dravidian Languages

The major Dravidian literary languages are:

  • Tamil.
  • Telugu.
  • Kannada.
  • Malayalam.
📌 Must-Memorise

Major Dravidian → Tamil + Telugu + Kannada + Malayalam

49. Tamil
  • Tamil is the principal language of Tamil Nadu.
  • It is also spoken in:
  • Puducherry.
  • Sri Lanka.
  • Several overseas Tamil communities.
  • It belongs to the Dravidian family.
50. Telugu
  • Telugu is principally spoken in:
  • Andhra Pradesh.
  • Telangana.
  • It belongs to the Dravidian family.
51. Kannada
  • Kannada is the principal language of Karnataka.
  • It belongs to the Dravidian family.
52. Malayalam
  • Malayalam is the principal language of Kerala.
  • It belongs to the Dravidian family.
53. Other Dravidian Languages

Examples include:

  • Tulu.
  • Kodava.
  • Toda.
  • Kota.
  • Gondi.
  • Kurukh.
54. Gondi
  • Gondi is a Dravidian language spoken among Gond communities in parts of central India.
  • This is an important reminder that Dravidian languages are not confined only to southern states.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Dravidian Languages → Not Restricted Only to South India

55. Kurukh
  • Kurukh is a Dravidian language associated with Oraon/Kurukh communities.
  • It is spoken in parts of eastern and central India.
56. Austroasiatic Languages
  • Austroasiatic languages occur mainly among tribal populations of central, eastern and northeastern India.
  • Important branches include:
  • Munda.
  • Mon-Khmer-related groups.
57. Munda Languages

Important Munda languages include:

  • Santali.
  • Mundari.
  • Ho.
58. Santali
  • Santali is spoken by the Santhal/Santal people.
  • It is concentrated in parts of:
  • Jharkhand.
  • West Bengal.
  • Odisha.
  • Bihar.
  • It belongs to the Austroasiatic family.
📌 Must-Memorise

Santali → Austroasiatic

59. Khasi
  • Khasi is spoken in Meghalaya.
  • It belongs to the Austroasiatic family.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Khasi Language → Austroasiatic

60. Tibeto-Burman Languages
  • Tibeto-Burman languages occur mainly in:
  • Northeastern India.
  • Himalayan regions.
  • They belong to the wider Sino-Tibetan language family.
61. Examples of Tibeto-Burman Languages

Examples include languages associated with:

  • Bodo.
  • Naga groups.
  • Mizo.
  • Meitei-related linguistic traditions.
  • Himalayan communities.
62. Bodo
  • Bodo is spoken mainly in Assam and adjoining regions.
  • It belongs to the Tibeto-Burman language group.
63. Mizo
  • Mizo is the dominant language of Mizoram.
  • It belongs to the Tibeto-Burman group.
64. Meitei / Manipuri
  • Meitei is the principal language of the Manipur Valley.
  • Manipuri/Meitei belongs to the Tibeto-Burman linguistic tradition.
65. Language and Physical Geography

Mountain barriers can:

  • Isolate communities.
  • Preserve small languages.
  • Increase linguistic diversity.

This is especially evident in northeastern India.

66. Language and Plains

Large plains favour:

  • Movement.
  • Trade.
  • Political integration.

Therefore, widespread regional languages often develop across plains.

67. Linguistic States
  • Reorganisation of states on linguistic lines strengthened the geographical association between major languages and state boundaries.
  • However, no state is linguistically completely homogeneous.
68. Eighth Schedule
  • The Eighth Schedule of the Constitution recognises 22 languages.
📌 Must-Memorise

Eighth Schedule → 22 Languages

69. Eighth Schedule Languages

The 22 languages are:

  • Assamese.
  • Bengali.
  • Bodo.
  • Dogri.
  • Gujarati.
  • Hindi.
  • Kannada.
  • Kashmiri.
  • Konkani.
  • Maithili.
  • Malayalam.
  • Manipuri.
  • Marathi.
  • Nepali.
  • Odia.
  • Punjabi.
  • Sanskrit.
  • Santali.
  • Sindhi.
  • Tamil.
  • Telugu.
  • Urdu.
70. Classical Languages — Geographic Importance

Several Indian languages have long literary traditions.

Tamil is especially important in TNPSC because of its ancient literary and cultural history.

71. Multilingualism
  • Multilingualism means use of more than one language by individuals or communities.
  • It is common throughout India.
72. Tribal Population — Basic Meaning
  • Tribal communities are indigenous or historically distinct social groups with specific cultural, linguistic and territorial traditions.
  • In constitutional and administrative terminology, recognised communities are referred to as Scheduled Tribes.
73. Scheduled Tribes
  • Scheduled Tribes are communities notified under constitutional provisions.
  • Their distribution is geographically uneven.
74. Major Tribal Regions of India

Large tribal concentrations occur in:

  • Central Indian tribal belt.
  • Northeastern India.
  • Western India.
  • Himalayan regions.
  • Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
  • Eastern and Western Ghats.
75. Central Indian Tribal Belt

The major tribal belt extends broadly through:

  • Rajasthan.
  • Gujarat.
  • Madhya Pradesh.
  • Maharashtra.
  • Chhattisgarh.
  • Jharkhand.
  • Odisha.
76. Northeast Tribal Region

Tribal communities form a major part of the population in several northeastern states.

Important groups include:

  • Nagas.
  • Mizos.
  • Khasis.
  • Garos.
  • Bodos.
  • Adis.
  • Apatanis.
  • Nyishis.
77. Gond
  • Gond is one of India's major tribal communities.
  • Gond populations occur mainly in central India.

Important regions include:

  • Madhya Pradesh.
  • Chhattisgarh.
  • Maharashtra.
  • Telangana.
  • Parts of Odisha.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gond → Central India

78. Gondwana
  • The historical-geographical term Gondwana is associated with regions inhabited by Gond communities.
  • It covers parts of central India.
79. Bhil
  • Bhils are a major tribal community of western and central India.
  • They are found mainly in:
  • Rajasthan.
  • Gujarat.
  • Madhya Pradesh.
  • Maharashtra.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhil → Rajasthan + Gujarat + MP + Maharashtra

80. Santhal / Santal
  • Santhals are concentrated mainly in:
  • Jharkhand.
  • West Bengal.
  • Odisha.
  • Bihar.
  • Santali belongs to the Austroasiatic language family.
📌 Must-Memorise

Santhal → Jharkhand–West Bengal–Odisha Belt

81. Munda
  • Munda communities are strongly associated with the Chotanagpur Plateau.
  • Jharkhand is an important centre.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Munda → Chotanagpur → Jharkhand

82. Oraon
  • Oraon communities are also known as Kurukh.
  • They are found mainly in:
  • Jharkhand.
  • Chhattisgarh.
  • Odisha.
  • Adjoining regions.
83. Ho
  • Ho communities are concentrated mainly in Jharkhand and adjoining Odisha.
  • Their language belongs to the Munda branch of Austroasiatic.
84. Baiga
  • Baiga communities are associated with central India.
  • Important concentrations occur in Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh.
85. Sahariya
  • Sahariya communities are found in parts of:
  • Madhya Pradesh.
  • Rajasthan.
86. Toda
  • Toda are an indigenous pastoral community of the Nilgiri Hills in Tamil Nadu.
  • They are traditionally associated with buffalo pastoralism.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Toda → Nilgiris → Buffalo Pastoralism

87. Toda Settlement
  • Traditional Toda settlements are called munds.
  • Their distinctive barrel-shaped huts are culturally important.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Toda Settlement → Mund

88. Kota
  • Kota are another indigenous community of the Nilgiris.
  • They have traditionally been associated with crafts and village occupations.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Kota → Nilgiris

89. Kurumba
  • Kurumba communities occur in the Nilgiri and adjoining Western Ghats region.
  • Traditional livelihoods included forest-based activities.
90. Irula
  • Irula communities are found in Tamil Nadu and adjoining states.
  • Important concentrations occur in:
  • Nilgiris.
  • Eastern Ghats foothills.
  • Northern Tamil Nadu.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Irula → Tamil Nadu Tribal Community

91. Paniya
  • Paniya communities occur in parts of the Nilgiris-Wayanad region.
  • They are found across Tamil Nadu and Kerala.
92. Kattunayakan
  • Kattunayakan communities are associated with forest regions of the Nilgiris and adjoining Western Ghats.
  • Traditional livelihoods include forest-resource collection.
93. Malayali Tribes of Tamil Nadu
  • Malayali tribal communities are concentrated in several Eastern Ghats hill systems of Tamil Nadu.
  • Important areas include:
  • Shevaroy Hills.
  • Kalrayan Hills.
  • Javadi Hills.
  • Kolli Hills.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Malayali Tribes → Tamil Nadu Eastern Ghats

94. Paliyan
  • Paliyan communities are associated with parts of the southern Western Ghats and Palani Hills.
95. Kani
  • Kani communities occur in the southern Western Ghats, particularly in the Agasthyamalai region of Tamil Nadu and Kerala.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Kani → Agasthyamalai

96. Tribal Geography of Tamil Nadu

Major tribal landscapes include:

  • Nilgiris.
  • Eastern Ghats.
  • Anaimalai.
  • Palani Hills.
  • Agasthyamalai.
  • Other Western Ghats regions.
97. Nilgiri Tribal Communities

Important groups include:

  • Toda.
  • Kota.
  • Kurumba.
  • Irula.
  • Paniya.
  • Kattunayakan.
📌 Must-Memorise

Nilgiris → Major Tribal Diversity Region

98. Naga Tribes
  • "Naga" refers to numerous distinct tribal groups of Nagaland and adjoining northeastern regions.
  • They possess different languages and cultural traditions.
99. Khasi
  • Khasi communities are concentrated in Meghalaya.
  • Khasi society is widely noted for matrilineal traditions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Khasi → Meghalaya → Matrilineal

100. Garo
  • Garos are concentrated mainly in western Meghalaya and adjoining areas.
  • Garo society also has matrilineal traditions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Garo → Meghalaya

101. Jaintia
  • Jaintia communities are associated with eastern Meghalaya.
  • Khasi, Garo and Jaintia hills form major cultural-geographical regions of Meghalaya.
102. Mizo
  • Mizo communities form the major population of Mizoram.
  • Their traditional settlement and culture developed in hill environments.
103. Bodo
  • Bodo communities are mainly concentrated in Assam.
  • They are associated especially with the Brahmaputra Valley and adjoining foothill areas.
104. Adi
  • Adi communities are associated with Arunachal Pradesh.
  • They inhabit parts of the eastern Himalayan region.
105. Apatani
  • Apatani communities are associated with the Ziro Valley of Arunachal Pradesh.
  • They are known for intensive wet-rice cultivation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Apatani → Ziro Valley → Arunachal Pradesh

106. Nyishi
  • Nyishi communities are among the important tribal groups of Arunachal Pradesh.
107. Lepcha
  • Lepcha communities are indigenous to parts of:
  • Sikkim.
  • Darjeeling region.
  • They are historically associated with the eastern Himalayas.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lepcha → Sikkim

108. Bhutia
  • Bhutia communities are associated mainly with Sikkim and Himalayan regions.
  • Their cultural links extend toward Tibetan traditions.
109. Monpa
  • Monpa communities occur mainly in western Arunachal Pradesh.
  • Tawang region is strongly associated with Monpa culture.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Monpa → Tawang

110. Tharu
  • Tharu communities inhabit the Terai region along the Himalayan foothills.
  • Important concentrations occur in:
  • Uttar Pradesh.
  • Uttarakhand.
  • Nepal border region.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tharu → Terai

111. Gujjar
  • Gujjar communities occur across northern and northwestern India.
  • Some groups traditionally practise pastoralism.
112. Bakarwal
  • Bakarwals are traditionally pastoral communities of Jammu and Kashmir.
  • They undertake seasonal movement with livestock.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bakarwal → Transhumant Pastoralism

113. Transhumance
  • Transhumance is seasonal movement of pastoral communities and livestock between different grazing grounds.
📌 Must-Memorise

Transhumance → Seasonal Pastoral Migration

114. Himalayan Transhumance

Pastoral groups move:

  • To higher pastures in summer.
  • To lower valleys in winter.
115. Gaddi
  • Gaddi pastoral communities are associated particularly with Himachal Pradesh.
  • Seasonal livestock movement is traditionally important.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Gaddi → Himachal Pradesh

116. Changpa
  • Changpa are nomadic or semi-nomadic pastoral communities of Ladakh.
  • They are associated with rearing goats that produce fine pashmina fibre.
📌 Must-Memorise

Changpa → Ladakh → Pashmina Goats

117. Pashmina
  • Pashmina is a very fine fibre obtained from specialised goats of the high-altitude Himalayan region.
118. Rabari
  • Rabari communities are traditionally pastoralists of western India.
  • They are especially associated with Gujarat and Rajasthan.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Rabari → Gujarat/Rajasthan Pastoralists

119. Tribal Livelihoods

Traditional tribal livelihoods may include:

  • Shifting cultivation.
  • Settled agriculture.
  • Pastoralism.
  • Hunting and gathering.
  • Forest-product collection.
  • Handicrafts.
120. Tribal Communities and Forests

Forests provide:

  • Food.
  • Fuel.
  • Fodder.
  • Medicine.
  • Housing materials.
  • Non-timber forest products.
121. Shifting Cultivation and Tribal Geography

Shifting cultivation is traditionally practised in some northeastern and hill regions.

Regional names include:

  • Jhum.
  • Podu.
  • Kumari.
  • Bewar.
122. Jhum
  • Jhum is especially associated with northeastern India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Jhum → Northeast India

123. Podu
  • Podu cultivation is associated with parts of:
  • Odisha.
  • Andhra Pradesh.
  • Telangana.
124. Tribal Settlements

Tribal settlements are influenced by:

  • Forests.
  • Hill slopes.
  • Water.
  • Agricultural land.
  • Security.
  • Transport access.
125. Tribal Isolation

Mountain and forest terrain historically reduced outside contact in many tribal areas.

This contributed to preservation of:

  • Languages.
  • Customs.
  • Traditional ecological knowledge.
126. Tribal Urbanisation
  • Tribal populations increasingly participate in:
  • Education.
  • Urban employment.
  • Industrial labour.
  • Tribal society is not static.
127. Traditional Ecological Knowledge
  • Indigenous and tribal communities often possess detailed knowledge of:
  • Forest plants.
  • Water sources.
  • Wildlife.
  • Seasonal cycles.
  • Agricultural practices.
128. Pastoralism
  • Pastoralism is a livelihood based substantially on livestock herding.
  • It is adapted to regions where crop cultivation is difficult.
129. Nomadic Pastoralism
  • Nomadic pastoralists move with livestock without a permanent agricultural base.
130. Semi-Nomadic Pastoralism
  • Semi-nomadic groups may maintain a permanent base while moving seasonally with livestock.
131. Pastoral Regions of India

Important pastoral landscapes include:

  • Rajasthan.
  • Gujarat.
  • Himalayas.
  • Ladakh.
  • Semi-arid Deccan.
132. Desert Pastoralism

The Thar Desert supports:

  • Camel.
  • Sheep.
  • Goat rearing.

Pastoral movement responds to water and pasture availability.

133. Mountain Pastoralism

Himalayan pastoralism depends on seasonal availability of:

  • Alpine meadows.
  • Lower winter grazing grounds.
134. Fishing Communities

Fishing communities are concentrated along:

  • Coastlines.
  • Estuaries.
  • Rivers.
  • Lakes.
  • Reservoirs.
135. Coastal Social Geography

Coastal livelihoods include:

  • Fishing.
  • Salt production.
  • Port labour.
  • Aquaculture.
  • Trade.
  • Tourism.
136. Tamil Nadu Fishing Settlements
  • Fishing settlements occur along the long Tamil Nadu coast.
  • Important coastal environments include:
  • Coromandel Coast.
  • Palk Bay.
  • Gulf of Mannar.
  • Kanyakumari coast.
137. Marine Livelihood Risks

Fishing communities face:

  • Cyclones.
  • Storm surges.
  • Coastal erosion.
  • Rough seas.
  • Changing fish availability.
138. Agricultural Communities

Agrarian settlement patterns differ according to:

  • Irrigation.
  • Crop type.
  • Landholding.
  • Soil.
  • Market access.
139. Kaveri Delta Social Geography

The Kaveri delta has:

  • Dense villages.
  • Long agricultural history.
  • Paddy-based economy.
  • Extensive irrigation networks.
140. Plantation Societies

Plantation regions often contain labour populations linked to:

  • Tea.
  • Coffee.
  • Rubber.

Examples include:

  • Assam tea belt.
  • Nilgiri plantations.
  • Kerala plantations.
141. Nilgiri Plantation Geography

Nilgiris combines:

  • Tribal settlements.
  • Tea estates.
  • Hill towns.
  • Forests.
  • Tourism.
142. Industrial Social Geography

Industries attract labour and create urban concentrations.

Important Indian industrial regions include:

  • Mumbai-Pune.
  • Ahmedabad-Vadodara.
  • Chotanagpur.
  • Chennai-Bengaluru corridor.
  • Coimbatore-Tiruppur belt.
143. Industrial Migration

Industrial regions attract:

  • Skilled workers.
  • Semi-skilled labour.
  • Construction workers.
  • Service workers.
144. Tiruppur Social Geography
  • Tiruppur's garment industry attracts workers from:
  • Other Tamil Nadu districts.
  • Other Indian states.
  • This creates a multilingual urban workforce.
145. Chennai Social Geography

  • Hospitals.
  • Public health centres.
  • Community facilities.
  • Drinking-water systems.

  • Urbanisation.

Gender geography examines spatial differences in:

  • Employment.
  • Education.
  • Mobility.
  • Access to resources.
  • Safety.

  • Migration.
  • Mortality.
  • Gender discrimination.
  • Employment structure.

  • Food culture.
  • Labour markets.

156. Cultural Diffusion

  • Assimilation occurs when a group increasingly adopts the cultural characteristics of another group.

  • A cultural region is an area sharing important cultural traits such as:

  • Architecture.
  • Customs.

  • A linguistic region is an area where a particular language or language group predominates.

Examples include:

225. TNPSC Traps

  • Language and race are not the same.
  • Language and religion are not the same.
  • India has several major language families.
  • Indo-Aryan and Dravidian are language families, not races.
  • Dravidian languages are not confined only to southern India.
  • Gondi and Kurukh are Dravidian languages spoken in central/eastern India.
  • Santali belongs to Austroasiatic, not Dravidian.
  • Khasi belongs to Austroasiatic.
  • Bodo and Mizo belong to Tibeto-Burman.

  • Scheduled Tribe is an administrative-constitutional category.
